fatal_errors: The proposed test at approximately 600 °C in an aqueous 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is not physically viable in an ordinary tribocorrosion cell; maintaining liquid water would require a specialized high-pressure apparatus that is not specified.

The central micro-galvanic FCC/σ-phase mechanism does not reconstruct the target L12/B2 alloy or the observed competition among depassivation, repassivation, tribolayer stability, and debris-assisted wear.

The prediction that the multiphase alloy degrades more than a single-phase baseline is opposite to the target result, in which the lamellar multiphase HEA substantially outperformed identically tested duplex stainless steel.

The proposed homogenized single-phase alloy of identical bulk composition is not shown to be thermodynamically attainable, and the required processing would alter grain size, residual stress, hardness, and other variables independently of phase multiplicity.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad theme of wear-induced passive-film rupture and corrosion–wear synergy, so it has limited problem alignment. It does not reproduce the studied material, thermal-shock treatment, DS2205 comparator, immersed reciprocating geometry, deionized-water environment, or 25–100 °C temperature dependence. It also misses the key nonmonotonic result: minimum degradation near 50 °C and increased degradation at 100 °C due to unstable oxide/tribolayer patches. The proposed experiment is directionally discriminating, but it neither cleanly separates wear, corrosion, and synergy nor controls processing-induced mechanical changes. The evidence concerns different laser-clad CoCrFeNiMo systems and mostly shows that refined dual-phase structures and oxide films can improve wear and corrosion resistance; it therefore does not establish that phase galvanic coupling causes greater coupled degradation in the proposed alloy. A strong falsification rule is stated, but it rests on an inadequately controlled and potentially infeasible baseline and test condition.
